title: Expanded Geometries and the Molecular Orbital Idea

pages.title: Why do some central atoms have five or six neighbours?

blocks.text: Methane’s four bonds are familiar, but PCl₅ and SF₆ require descriptions with five and six directions. Their observed geometries extend the simple examples without changing the need for consistent electron accounting.
The textbook labels these patterns sp³d and sp³d². We will learn the geometries, then introduce a molecular-orbital approach that describes electrons over an entire molecule.

pages.transition: Describe the five-direction geometry using axial and equatorial sites.

pages.title: Describe five directions in PCl₅

blocks.text: The textbook’s sp³d scheme combines one s, three p and one d orbital to describe five directions in a trigonal bipyramid. Three equatorial bonds lie 120° apart; two axial bonds are perpendicular to that plane.
The axial and equatorial environments differ. Axial pairs experience three 90° interactions with equatorial pairs, so the axial P–Cl bonds are longer and weaker in the simple account.

Equatorial means around the central plane, like three points around a horizontal triangle. Axial means along the line through the centre above and below that plane. These labels distinguish positions within one trigonal bipyramid, not different molecules.

pages.transition: Contrast it with six equivalent directions in an octahedron.

pages.title: Describe six directions in SF₆

blocks.text: The sp³d² label describes six directions to the corners of an octahedron. In SF₆, six equivalent S–F bond directions give adjacent angles 90° and opposite angles 180°.
Octahedral means six vertices, not eight bonded atoms: the name refers to the eight faces of the geometric solid. Distinguish the number of faces from the number of bond directions.

pages.transition: State what the traditional hybridisation labels do and do not establish.

pages.title: Keep the textbook label and its limits clear

blocks.text: For this course, associate PCl₅ with trigonal bipyramidal geometry and the textbook sp³d label; associate SF₆ with octahedral geometry and sp³d². These labels summarise a model of direction.

Clarification: modern explanations of hypervalent main-group bonding do not require literal extensive occupation of low-energy d hybrids. The observed shapes are reliable; the historical orbital-mixing explanation should not be treated as a direct measurement.

pages.transition: A molecule-wide orbital picture addresses different electronic questions.

pages.title: Ask whether electrons belong only to one bond

blocks.text: A local overlap picture is useful, but some observations require a molecule-wide description. Molecular orbital theory places electrons in orbitals associated with the whole molecule rather than only one atom.
An atomic orbital is centred on one atom; a molecular orbital can extend over several nuclei. It is still a wave function, and electron occupation obeys quantum rules.

pages.transition: Construct the new states from compatible atomic functions.

pages.title: Combine two atomic wave functions

blocks.text: In the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals approach, LCAO, two suitable atomic orbitals generate two molecular orbitals. Addition of matching phases increases density between nuclei; subtraction creates a node between them.
The two combinations are bonding and antibonding orbitals. The total number of orbitals is conserved. A star, as in σ*, marks an antibonding orbital; it is not an electron charge.

pages.transition: Interpret how the two combinations change energy and density.

pages.title: Interpret bonding and antibonding energies

blocks.text: A bonding molecular orbital lies lower in energy than the combining atomic orbitals and favours holding the nuclei together. An antibonding orbital lies higher and reduces the stabilisation when occupied.
Do not picture antibonding as a separate chemical bond with negative length. It is an allowed electronic state with a different density distribution and energy.

pages.transition: Identify which atomic functions can combine effectively.

pages.title: Choose atomic orbitals that can combine

blocks.text: Effective combinations require compatible energies, suitable symmetry about the molecular axis and significant overlap. An H 1s orbital combines effectively with another H 1s in H₂.
Orbitals of very different energy or incompatible symmetry do not mix strongly in the simple construction. Being drawn near each other on an energy diagram is not sufficient.

pages.transition: Fill the simplest molecule to connect the construction with bonding.

pages.title: Fill the H₂ molecular orbitals

blocks.text: Two H atoms contribute two electrons. They occupy the lower σ1s bonding orbital with opposite spins, leaving σ*1s empty. Bonding electrons therefore outweigh antibonding electrons.
The molecule is stabilised and all electrons are paired. This elementary example connects molecular occupation with bonding before more complicated second-period diagrams are considered.

Place a third electron into the H₂-derived MO scheme to make H₂⁻ in the simple model. It must enterσ*1s afterσ1s is filled, so net stabilisation is smaller and one electron is unpaired. The example illustrates occupation, not a claim of ordinary bulk stability.

pages.transition: Keep the geometry model distinct from molecular electron occupation.

pages.title: Distinguish geometry labels from molecule-wide states

blocks.text: The five- and six-domain geometries describe PCl₅ and SF₆; the traditional hybrid labels are course models. Molecular orbitals instead describe delocalised electronic states formed from compatible atomic functions.
Keep orbital count, electron count and energy occupation consistent. The next step is to use molecular occupations to predict bond order and magnetic behaviour.

questions.question: How many axial bonds are in trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅?
questions.answer: Two axial bonds; the other three are equatorial.

questions.question: Why are axial P–Cl bonds different from equatorial ones?
questions.answer: Their electron regions have more 90° interactions, giving a less favourable environment and longer, weaker axial bonds in the simple model.

questions.question: How many bond directions does an octahedron have?
How many MOs arise from two combining AOs?
What does the star in σ* mean?
What conditions favour effective orbital mixing?
questions.answer: Comparable energy, compatible symmetry and appreciable overlap.

questions.question: Why does H₂ have net bonding?
questions.answer: Its two electrons occupy the bondingσ1s orbital while antibondingσ*1s remains empty.
